claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating initially forms an FCC solid solution with low dislocation density and no HCP phase.
Above 900 K, deformation transitions from dislocation-controlled plasticity to grain-boundary- or interface-mediated deformation.
The high-temperature response is not caused by a specific martensitic transformation.
Thermal energy above 900 K overcomes a stacking-fault-energy barrier and causes amorphization onset and loss of structural integrity.
The proposed simulations use a 30 Å indentation depth and 10 m/s indentation velocity at 900, 1000, 1100, and 1200 K.
An inert atmosphere isolates thermal and mechanical effects from tribo-oxidation.
Rapid stacking-fault accumulation produces lattice disordering and localized amorphization.
Thermal activation breaks down dislocation-forest hardening above 900 K.
High temperature unlocks dislocation locks analogous to Lomer-Cottrell locks observed in HEAs.
Above 900 K, thermal energy prevents dislocation annihilation and drives the material toward a disordered or amorphous state.
High-temperature RHEAs exhibit lattice-distortion-dominated behavior and shifts in deformation mechanism.
A disordered, low-shear-strength surface layer increases adhesion and plowing resistance, producing the friction spike.
Above 900 K, the coefficient of friction spikes nonlinearly while hardness and wear resistance drop precipitously.
The friction and wear changes coincide with increased amorphous-atom fraction or stacking-fault density and reduced long-range crystalline order.
The high-temperature degradation occurs without a significant increase in HCP phase fraction.
At 300–600 K, dislocation density decreases slightly, increasing elastic modulus while the alloy remains FCC and free of amorphization.
The stable low-temperature FCC state produces stable friction and wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to polycrystalline material, where grain-boundary sliding dominates, or below 900 K.
Artificially increasing stacking-fault energy will suppress stacking-fault accumulation and amorphization onset.
Persistence of the friction spike and wear loss under suppressed stacking faults, with low amorphous-atom count, would falsify the proposed disordering mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts rapid stacking-fault accumulation but also expects no significant or negligible HCP population. In an FCC alloy, common-neighbor analysis generally labels atoms associated with intrinsic stacking faults as HCP-like, so extensive stacking faults should increase the measured HCP-atom count even without a bulk HCP martensitic phase.

The main hypothesis invokes grain-boundary-mediated deformation in a single crystal, while the boundary statement associates grain-boundary sliding with polycrystalline material and says the hypothesis may not apply there. The alternative reference to interface-mediated deformation partly mitigates but does not resolve this inconsistency.
